tagline: A border road follows the Dead River toward Sugarloaf and Kingfield
intro: Route 27 connects Coburn Gore at the Quebec border with Eustis, Stratton and Carrabassett Valley, passing Sugarloaf Mountain on the way to Kingfield. North of Eustis, the road parallels the North Branch Dead River, which flows from Chain of Ponds. MaineDOT records a state scenic-byway designation in 1971, beginning 0.80 mile north of the Routes 16 and 27 junction in Kingfield. Sugarloaf is Maine’s third-highest peak, after Katahdin’s Baxter and Hamlin peaks. The scenic corridor occupies the northern part of a much longer numbered highway, which begins at Newagen in Southport.

The river corridor carried a much earlier journey. In 1775, Benedict Arnold’s expedition ascended the North Branch through Chain of Ponds toward Quebec’s Chaudière River. Part of that expedition route now lies beneath Flagstaff Lake, enlarged when the Dead River was dammed in the twentieth century. The enlarged lake also drowned the meeting of the North and South branches of the Dead River at Eustis in 1950.

Drive south from Coburn Gore toward Eustis, then Stratton, where Route 16 joins Route 27. Flagstaff Lake is one of Eustis’s sites of interest. The shared highway continues through Carrabassett Valley past Sugarloaf to Kingfield. There, the Carrabassett meets its West Branch in the village.

moments.title: Coburn Gore
moments.text: Two houses across Route 27 from the inspection building explain the remoteness of this border station: it was built with housing for its principal officers. The 1931 station belonged to a federal program to improve border security and create Depression-era jobs. Prohibition smuggling, growing automobile use and immigration quotas helped drive that program. The brick-veneered inspection building retains much of its Colonial Revival styling. Its central lobby separates immigration and customs service areas. Garage wings extend from either side of the main building, and a metal canopy shelters two lanes where vehicles are processed at the crossing.
moments.notice: The inspection building and the officers’ residences occupy opposite sides of Route 27.

moments.title: Flagstaff Lake
moments.text: Flagstaff Lake covers parts of four abandoned townships: Flagstaff, Bigelow, Dead River and Carrying Place. The lake was smaller before Long Falls Dam impounded the Dead River in 1950, enlarging it into a reservoir. The project had been contested since 1923, with Central Maine Power president Walter Wyman opposed by legislator and future governor Percival Proctor Baxter. The dam generates no electricity itself. It regulates water for eight downstream Kennebec hydropower projects and controls flooding. The Bigelow Mountain Range overlooks the southern shore. The North and South branches meet in the lake, forming the Dead River.
moments.notice: The Bigelow Mountain Range rises along the lake’s southern shore.

moments.title: Kingfield
moments.text: The Carrabassett River powered Kingfield’s sawmills, flour mill, tannery and rake factory; those mills are now closed. The town’s Stanley twins, Francis and Freelan, manufactured photographic dry plates and the Stanley Steamer automobile. Their sister Chansonetta photographed rural life, and the Stanley Museum celebrates the family’s work. In the early 1950s, local residents began developing Sugarloaf as a ski resort. Kingfield is now a gateway to the mountain. The twins also designed the Amos G. Winter House, whose original heating system used a railroad engine boiler. Steam powered more than their automobiles.
